Maricopa County bills it, not the city. The Maricopa County Assessor decides each parcel's value and classification. Billing and collection fall to the Maricopa County Treasurer, who takes in money for more than 1,800 tax districts (state, county, cities and towns, schools, community colleges and special districts) and distributes it.

So a Phoenix owner calls one of two offices, depending on the question.

  • Assessor: what your Notice of Valuation says, your home's legal class, appeals, notices of claim and personal exemptions. Visit 301 W Jefferson St, Phoenix, AZ 85003, or use the appeals line, 602-506-3406.
  • Treasurer: what you owe, how to pay, refunds, delinquent notices and tax lien questions.

The city picks its own rates yet never assesses your home or takes your payment. What it levies is one line among the others on your county bill.

Payment is split between October 1 and the next March 1 (A.R.S. 42-18052). Delinquency begins after 5:00 p.m. on November 1 for the first half and May 1 for the second, and a weekend or holiday pushes that to 5:00 p.m. the next business day.

This year it applied. With November 1 on a Sunday, 2026's first half went delinquent after 5 p.m. Monday, November 2, so any unpaid first half is late now. Next spring, May 1, 2027 lands on a Saturday and the second-half deadline should roll to Monday, May 3, 2027.

Interest on late tax is simple, 16 percent annually, and any part of a month is billed as a full month (A.R.S. 42-18053). Pay the entire year by December 31 and none is collected. If you haven't paid your 2026 first half, you therefore have until Thursday, December 31, 2026 to pay both halves clean. Small bills of $100 or less are due in one piece on October 1 and go delinquent after December 31.

Phoenix had an estimated 1,665,481 residents in July 2025. Among the city's 15 urban villages are Ahwatukee Foothills, Camelback East, Laveen, Maryvale, Encanto and South Mountain. Owners occupy 57.3 percent of homes, and the median owner-occupied home is valued at $420,700.

Housing varies a great deal within city limits, and the school, community college and special districts on your bill follow the parcel. Homes in Maryvale and Ahwatukee Foothills share a city without sharing a bill. The Assessor's site shows which districts cover your address; houses only a mile apart may carry different total rates.

The city's published notice for 2026-27 proposed a primary rate of $1.2652 per $100 of assessed valuation, slightly down from $1.2658, and a secondary rate of $0.7745, down from $0.8141. The city said that even with the lower primary rate, rising assessed values would still lift primary taxes for the average owner by 2.79 percent. Ask the Treasurer which rates are in effect.

Primary and secondary tax pay for different things.

  • Primary tax supports General Fund services such as police and fire, parks and recreation, libraries and community centers. State law limits how fast a city's primary levy can grow (A.R.S. 42-17051).
  • Secondary tax pays bonded debt service for facilities such as libraries, police and fire stations, storm drains and parks.

That covers just the city. County, school district and community college rates are added on top, so the full bill exceeds the city's line. Maricopa County posts rate and levy tables for every taxing jurisdiction on its Tax Levy and Rates page.

File with the Maricopa County Assessor no more than 60 days after the mailing date of your Notice of Valuation (A.R.S. 42-16051). Late winter is when notices arrive. Find the mail date printed on yours and count forward 60 days.

Three different filings are described on the Assessor's appeals page. Picking the wrong one wastes time.

  • Real property appeal: use it if you think full cash value or classification is incorrect. The Petition for Review of Valuation (AZDOR Form 82130R) goes in by mail or in person, and emailed appeals aren't accepted.
  • Notice of Claim: use it when the record has a plain error, such as the wrong square footage. It looks back over this year and three earlier ones, and an approved claim may bring a refund via the Treasurer.
  • Residential Legal Class Change: use it once a home becomes your primary residence. You'll need documents showing your name at the property address, namely a driver's license, voter registration, or a tax return address page paired with a vehicle registration or utility bill.

Attach evidence to any of them. An appeal lacking appraisals, comparable sales or similar documents can be denied.

Personal exemptions for widowed, totally disabled and veteran owners come from the Assessor's Valuation Relief division. February 28 is the application deadline, extended to September 1 for those with an approved Exemption Deadline Waiver. All of them require Arizona residency and household income below the statutory limit.

  • Widowed or totally disabled: up to $4,873 off the limited property value.
  • Veteran with a service-connected disability under 100 percent, or a nonservice-connected disability: up to $4,873, multiplied by the disability percentage.
  • Veteran with a 100 percent service-connected rating: the primary residence is fully exempt when every requirement, income included, is met.

The income cap is $39,865 for households with no children under 18, and $47,826 where children under 18 or disabled children lived in the home the prior year. Social Security, military pensions and VA disability payments don't count as income. Call 602-506-3406 before applying, because buying or selling property can end eligibility.

Plan to settle back taxes by closing at the latest. Under A.R.S. 42-18104, a county treasurer may sell one lien covering every delinquent year on the property. The title company can pull the balance and list it on the settlement statement.

A few steps keep closing on schedule.

  • Request a payoff figure from the escrow officer, with interest counted to the closing date.
  • An open first half for 2026 has been accruing interest from November 2.
  • Paid off a mortgage recently? The Treasurer can explain the waiver in A.R.S. 42-18053(C): it applies to a delinquency within a year of a mortgage or deed of trust release, requires board of supervisors approval, and works once per property.

Your deed is filed with the Maricopa County Recorder, whose staff won't give legal advice, fill in documents or notarize. Reach recording services at 602-506-3535. The steps are identical for a cash buyer or a financed one.

faqs.q: Does Phoenix itself collect my property tax?
faqs.a: No. Maricopa County's Treasurer bills and collects it, including the city's portion, and the Assessor sets your value. The city's rate is one line on that bill.

faqs.q: What is the last day to pay 2026 Phoenix property tax without interest?
faqs.a: December 31, 2026, covering the full year. A.R.S. 42-18053 waives interest on a full-year payment made by December 31 of the tax year. Paying only the first half after November 2 leaves interest running on what's unpaid.

faqs.q: What interest rate hits late Maricopa County property tax?
faqs.a: Sixteen percent annually, simple, from the delinquency date until paid, with part of a month counted whole. After a mortgage release, the treasurer may waive interest once per property if the board approves.

faqs.q: Can I still appeal my Phoenix home value?
faqs.a: Yes, if you file within 60 days of the mail date on your Notice of Valuation. For a plain factual error, such as wrong square footage, a Notice of Claim can reach back three prior tax years.

faqs.q: Do I have to pay Phoenix property tax before I sell?
faqs.a: Clear it at or before closing, with interest in the payoff. Your title officer or the Maricopa County Treasurer can give the exact amount for your parcel.
